Probabilistic Machine Learning
CS 691 · IIT Gandhinagar · Semester I, 2022–23
This course treats machine learning as inference under uncertainty. It moves from Bayes' rule, maximum likelihood and MAP estimation through approximate inference (Laplace, Monte Carlo, MCMC and variational methods) to Bayesian neural networks, Gaussian processes, latent-variable models, active learning, Bayesian optimisation and diffusion models. Assignments are written in JAX with TensorFlow Probability, and a project carries most of the grade.

  InstructorProf. Nipun Batra
  Emailnipun.batra@iitgn.ac.in
  ClassesThursday, 12:00–1:30 pm, 7/102; Friday, 2:00–3:30 pm, 7/105
  Google ClassroomClass code u7jjtu2
  Teaching assistantZeel B Patel
  PrerequisitesMathematics for ML, a prior ML course such as ES 654, and good Python programming (details)



Course record
This offering ran from August to November 2022. Its slides, notebooks and assignments remain available.

  Lectures23
  Assignments4
  Projects14 ideas
  Notebooks12, on GitHub

All dates


Lectures

  1–6Introduction to probabilistic ML6 lectures
  7–12Approximate inference6 lectures
  13–14Bayesian neural networks2 lectures
  15–16Gaussian processes2 lectures
  17–18Unsupervised learning2 lectures
  19–20Active learning and Bayesian optimisation2 lectures
  21–23Autoencoders, hierarchical and generative models3 lectures
  +Additional material1 topic


  All 23 lectures




Questions
What does the course cover?

  Probability refresher: probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, joint distributions, sampling from different distributions (for example with the Box–Muller transform), uncertainty modelling, and information-theoretic concepts such as KL divergence and entropy.
  Bayesian concept learning: likelihood, prior and posterior; maximum likelihood (MLE) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation; full Bayesian estimation with conjugate priors (the Beta–Bernoulli model for a coin toss, the Normal–Normal model for the parameters of a Normal distribution).
  Bayesian supervised methods: for regression, Bayesian linear regression and robust linear regression through alternative likelihoods (Laplace, Student-t); for classification, Bayesian logistic regression and Bayesian naive Bayes.
  Latent-variable modelling: Gaussian mixture models and probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA).
  Approximate inference: sampling (rejection sampling, importance sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo, Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs sampling, the No-U-Turn Sampler) and variational inference (mean field, the evidence lower bound, the reparameterisation trick, stochastic VI, automatic differentiation VI).
  Gaussian processes: the multivariate Normal distribution and its properties, kernels, GP regression and classification, approximate inference and sparse GPs.
  Bayesian optimisation and active learning: query by committee, uncertainty sampling, expected model change; acquisition functions, GP-based and random-forest-based Bayesian optimisation.
  Probabilistic deep learning: MC dropout, deep ensembles, Bayesian neural networks and deep GPs.

What should I know before the course?

  Mathematics for ML: the recommended reading is the Mathematics for Machine Learning book.
  A prior ML course: ES 654 at IIT Gandhinagar or equivalent.
  Good programming skills in Python and familiarity with NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and scikit-learn. The recommended reading is the Python Data Science Handbook.

How is the course graded?Assignments 20%, quizzes 20% and the project 60%. Each quiz covers everything from the previous quiz up to the day of the quiz. See Assessment.
How are assignments done?In groups of two, as a single Jupyter notebook, using TensorFlow Probability with the JAX substrate for distributions and JAX for automatic differentiation and vectorised code. Draw insights from your results rather than only presenting answers. See Assignments.
Is there a project?Yes, and it is worth 60% of the grade. The Projects page lists ideas, from Bayesian unlearning and Stein variational inference to deep GPs and neural processes for energy disaggregation and air quality.

References
Textbooks:

  Kevin P. Murphy, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press, 2012
  Kevin P. Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction, MIT Press, 2022
  Kevin P. Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics, MIT Press, 2023
  Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning
  Allen B. Downey, Think Bayes: Bayesian Statistics in Python, Green Tea Press, 2012
  David Barber, Bayesian Reasoning and Machine Learning, Cambridge University Press, 2012
  Carl Edward Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press, 2006
  Richard McElreath, Statistical Rethinking, CRC Press, 2020

Similar courses:

  Probabilistic Machine Learning by Piyush Rai, IIT Kanpur

title: Assignment 2
text:
Dataset
Create the following datasets to be used in the following questions

Dataset 1

import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax
x = jnp.linspace(-2, 2, 100)
f = 3*x + 2.0
eps = 0.5*jax.random.normal(key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0), shape=(100, ))
y = f + eps

Dataset 2

import jax.numpy as jnp
import jax
x = jnp.linspace(-2, 2, 100)
f = 3*x + 2.0
eps = 0.5*jax.random.normal(key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0), shape=(100, ))
y = f + eps
y = y.at[1].set(y[1] + 3)
y = y.at[30].set(y[30] + 1)

title: Assignment 2
text:
Questions

Assume scale=1 for the likelihood noise, learn the MLE parameters for Dataset 1 assuming Normal likelihood. [0.5 marks]
Assume scale=1 for the likelihood noise, learn the MLE parameters for Dataset 2 assuming Normal likelihood. [0.5 marks]
Learn the MLE parameters for Dataset 1 assuming Normal likelihood. Do not assume scale and also estimate it using MLE. You may prefer to learn log(scale) as a part of your optimisation procedure. Plot predicted function along with two scale (\(\mu \pm 2\sigma\)) band to show likelihood noise. [0.5 marks]
Repeat question 3 for Dataset 2. [0.5 marks]
Assume scale=1 for the likelihood noise, learn the MAP parameters for Dataset 1 assuming Normal likelihood and a Normal prior: \(p(\theta) = \mathcal{N}(0, b^2 I)\). Show the effect of varying b on the MAP parameters and the learnt function. [1 mark]
Repeat question 5, but instead of Normal prior choose a Laplace prior [0.5 marks]
Repeat question 3 for Dataset 2 but instead of Normal likelihood, Student-t likelihood with varying degrees of freedom. You should manually vary the degree of freedom in a range (you should choose the range based on the insights). [1 mark]
Implement Logistic regression using Bernoulli likelihood and learn the MLE and MAP parameters for Dataset 3. For MAP, assume normal prior. Also plot contours/surfaces of predictive mean and variance.[1.5 marks]

Use a subset of 5,000 images (500 images per class) from MNIST dataset and train a simple (deterministic)CNN model in Flax. Report the predicted accuracy on a separately kept 1,000 images test set (100 images per class). Also, report the predicted probabilities for wrongly classified examples. What can you conclude? Now, use the trained model on a set of 1,000 images on Fashion MNIST dataset. What can you conclude? [1.5 marks]
Modify the above CNN to include MC dropout as way to get uncertainty from the final dense layer. Rerun above experiments and report conclusions. [2 marks]
